name: Pomegranate
summary: A deciduous multi-stem shrub or small tree with ornamental flowers and edible arils. Cultivar and seasonal conditions affect fruit color, quality, and harvest; no cultivar is specified.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Punica granatum. NC State describes the species and lists named cultivars separately; this entry does not represent Nana or Salavatski.

growth.short: Deciduous perennial shrub or small tree
growth.guidance: NC State reports about 10–12 ft tall and 8–10 ft wide in its regional profile. These are outdoor landscape dimensions, not a container-size promise.

cultivation.short: Sun, drainage, and more even moisture near fruiting
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports sun to partial shade, moisture and good drainage. UGA's Georgia production guide recommends adequate soil moisture and warns that drought followed by rain or excessive fall irrigation can contribute to fruit splitting. These are outdoor, region-scoped observations and do not establish hydroponic suitability.

harvest.short: Use cultivar-aware maturity cues and clip the fruit
harvest.guidance: UGA says maturity depends on sugar, acid, and rind color, which varies by season and cultivar; its numeric indices are specific to 'Wonderful' and are not assigned here. Clip near the fruit base rather than pulling, and handle gently because impacts can crack fruit. Arils are edible fresh or used for juice.

propagation.short: Hardwood cuttings can clone a plant; seedlings do not preserve cultivar identity
propagation.guidance: UGA Extension describes hardwood cuttings as a preferred propagation method and also notes that seed-grown trees take longer to bear. A seedling from a named cultivar is not the same cultivar. This is regional propagation guidance; the separate Seed Profile governs seed-to-seedling establishment.

management.short: Prune lightly and maintain an open, supported canopy
management.guidance: UGA reports annual pruning to manage suckers and maintain structure, with major pruning in winter before bud break and lighter sucker removal in summer. Heavy pruning can remove older fruiting wood and reduce yield; support branches carrying heavy fruit. This is Georgia production guidance, not a universal home-garden calendar.

problems.short: Fruit set may be unreliable in humid regions
problems.guidance: NC State lists possible scale, whiteflies, mealybugs, leaf spot, fruit blotch and root rot. UGA also documents sunscald and fruit splitting linked with uneven moisture; humid bloom can impair fruit set in its Georgia context. These are scouting risks, not guaranteed outcomes or cultivar resistance claims.

name: Starfruit
summary: An evergreen tropical fruit tree with ribbed, star-shaped fruit. UF/IFAS reports ripe-fruit, pruning and landscape guidance for South Florida; this species-level entry does not assign a named cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Averrhoa carambola. UF/IFAS describes multiple cultivars separately; none is assigned here.

growth.short: Spreading tropical tree, about 22–33 ft in the UF/IFAS account
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes a small-to-medium evergreen tree about 22–33 ft tall and 20–25 ft wide in its Florida landscape account. It may lose some or all leaves in cooler locations. These are outdoor dimensions, not indoor/container sizes.

cultivation.short: Full sun, wind protection and well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends a sunny, wind-protected site and well-drained soil. Young trees need regular establishment watering; mature landscape trees are irrigated through flowering and harvest. This is not a hydroponic prescription.

care.short: Selective pruning can control size; avoid routine severe cuts
care.guidance: UF/IFAS says selective pruning can maintain mature landscape trees around 6–12 ft and reduce shading of lower canopy branches; it advises not removing the lower branches. The publication also describes specialized pruning to induce off-season flowering in South Florida, which is not presented here as a routine home-garden instruction.

harvest.short: Pick when the furrows turn yellow while rib tips remain green
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS says fruit does not gain sugar after picking: for best sweetness, harvest when the furrow between ribs changes from green to yellow while rib tips remain green. It reports a broad June–February window in South Florida, with cultivar-dependent peaks; that calendar is not universal.

propagation.guidance: UF/IFAS reports carambola cultivars are generally grafted on seedling rootstocks and documents veneer grafting and chip budding. Seedlings do not establish a named cultivar identity.

safety.guidance: UF/IFAS warns that people with diagnosed kidney disease should avoid star fruit unless their physician says it is safe. This is a dietary caution, not a plant-handling hazard.

problems.short: Excessively wet soil can lead to root rot and decline
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS associates overly wet or flooded conditions with root rot and tree decline, including reduced vigor, leaf drop, dieback and smaller or fewer fruits. It also documents scale and fruit pests in Florida; local diagnosis is appropriate before treatment.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: A Florida landscape publication does not demonstrate indoor hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: UF/IFAS describes a small-to-medium tree with spreading growth.

height.reason: Outdoor dimensions do not represent indoor/container form.

spread.reason: Outdoor dimensions do not establish indoor footprint.

spacing.reason: The outdoor landscape distance is not pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Pawpaw
summary: A deciduous eastern North American understory fruit tree with custard-like fruit. It is distinct from tropical papaya and needs pollen from a genetically different plant for reliable fruit set.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Asimina triloba and lists Annona triloba as a synonym. The common name pawpaw here is not tropical papaya (Carica papaya).

growth.guidance: NC State describes a native deciduous tree of woodland settings. Full sun favors fruiting, though it tolerates dappled sun and partial shade; flowers are self-incompatible and need a genetically different pollen donor.

pollination.short: A genetically different plant is usually needed for fruit set
pollination.guidance: Alabama Extension says pawpaws are usually not self-fertile and recommends at least two cultivars with overlapping bloom. A single clonal grove may not provide cross-pollination. Hand pollination is laborious and is not presented as a routine requirement when natural pollinators are present.

cultivation.guidance: NC State reports preference for acidic soil that retains moisture but drains well. It tolerates occasional moisture, not permanently saturated conditions. This does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

harvest.short: Pick as fruit first softens and handle gently
harvest.guidance: Alabama Extension says pawpaws soften rapidly at ripeness, may shift from darker green toward lighter green or yellow depending on cultivar, and bruise easily. Check trees frequently during the regional harvest period and pick when flesh first softens; unripe fruit can cause gastrointestinal distress. Alabama's July–September dates are not a universal calendar. NC State reports contact dermatitis for some people.

propagation.short: Use grafted trees for named-cultivar fruit; seedlings vary
propagation.guidance: Alabama Extension describes pawpaw propagation by seed or grafting and notes that seed-grown trees vary from the parent. Grafted scions from named cultivars are used when predictable fruit characteristics are the goal; digging and transplanting root suckers is usually unsuccessful. Seed stratification and sowing instructions belong in the Seed Profile, not here.

problems.guidance: NC State notes root suckers can become troublesome. Monitor the spread of suckers around established trees and remove unwanted shoots as appropriate; the source does not prescribe a universal removal schedule.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Woodland fruit-tree guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The existing compatibility habit vocabulary does not represent understory trees without adding unsupported precision.

spacing.reason: Landscape spacing is not pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor shade tolerance is not an indoor light tier.

name: American Persimmon
summary: A large deciduous North American fruit tree. Its fruit is strongly astringent when unripe and sweet when fully soft; distinct from Asian persimmon.

identity.short: Accepted North American species; distinct from D. kaki
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Diospyros virginiana. NC State lists American and common persimmon as names for this taxon; it is not D. kaki.

growth.short: Large deciduous tree; sexes usually separate
growth.guidance: NC State reports 30–80 ft height and 20–35 ft width in landscape settings and says trees are usually dioecious, with occasional perfect flowers. These are not container dimensions.

cultivation.short: Full sun to partial shade; moist, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State describes best growth in moist, well-drained sandy soil and tolerance of broader conditions. The large tree and deep taproot make this a landscape fruit identity, not an indoor hydroponic crop.

harvest.short: Wait until fruit is soft before eating
harvest.guidance: NC State says unripe fruit is astringent and soft ripe fruit is sweet. Its regional page reports fall fruiting and notes seed-grown trees may take 4–9 years to bear.

propagation.short: Seed, root cuttings and grafting are listed; protocol unresolved
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed, root cutting and grafting but no complete home sowing procedure. Seed is a documented route; establishment details remain insufficient for Seed Profile V0.

care.short: Control root suckers if a spreading colony is not wanted
care.guidance: NC State Extension notes mature trees produce root suckers that can become a weed problem. Monitor around the established tree and remove unwanted suckers; the source does not prescribe a routine canopy-pruning program for this species.

problems.short: Sex expression and fruit maturity matter
problems.guidance: NC State describes usually separate male and female trees and warns that green fruit is astringent. Root suckers may become a weed problem; no disease resistance is claimed.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Large outdoor tree guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The source lists several tree forms; no single compatibility habit can be assigned to this identity.

height.reason: Landscape dimensions are not container/indoor dimensions.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing is not pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure is not an indoor light tier.

name: Asian Persimmon
summary: A deciduous East Asian fruit tree with diverse fruit types and cultivars. No named cultivar or astringency class is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Diospyros kaki. NC State lists Fuyu and Jiro as examples of named cultivars; this species-level record does not represent either one.

growth.short: Deciduous fruit tree, about 20–30 ft in cited landscape profile
growth.guidance: NC State reports a 20–30 ft landscape height and describes a deciduous tree with glossy leaves and notable yellow-to-red autumn color. These are regional outdoor observations, not indoor dimensions or a cultivar-specific size guarantee.

cultivation.short: Full sun; moist, well-drained loam in regional guidance
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports best growth in full sun and moist, well-drained loam and gives a regional cold-limit context. This does not establish indoor or hydroponic performance.

flowering.short: Cream female flowers and pink male clusters bloom in spring
flowering.guidance: NC State describes solitary cream-white female flowers and pink male flowers in clusters of three. Its page places general bloom around mid-April in North Carolina; late frost may damage bloom, and local timing can differ.

pollination.short: Sex expression and fruit set vary; another variety is not always required
pollination.guidance: NC State says trees are usually dioecious, though some have both male and female flowers and some have perfect flowers. The species can also set seedless fruit without pollination. Planting more than one variety is recommended when larger yields are the goal, but is not required for fruit set. This entry names no variety or individual tree sex, so it cannot promise a crop or prescribe a pollinizer.

harvest.guidance: NC State describes non-astringent varieties that can be sliced and eaten raw. Because no cultivar is identified, this trait is not assigned to every D. kaki plant. Its general page says trees may take 4–6 years to begin fruiting and that a heavy crop may be followed by a smaller one; these are broad species-page expectations, not a guaranteed schedule for an individual tree.

propagation.short: Seed and grafting are listed; no seed-starting protocol
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and grafting but does not give a home seed-starting procedure. Seedlings are not identified as named cultivars, and cultivar fruit traits remain unresolved.

care.short: Remove unwanted root suckers; annual pruning is not required
care.guidance: NC State Extension says this species does not require annual pruning but produces root suckers that should be removed unless a naturalized effect is wanted. This is species-level landscape guidance; no cultivar-specific training system is assigned.

problems.short: Scale, mealybug, leaf spot and fruit drop are possible
problems.guidance: NC State lists these problems and notes fruit drop can be messy; root suckers may need removal.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor fruit-tree guidance does not establish indoor hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The species is described as a tree, but the current compatibility habit vocabulary does not include tree form.

height.reason: Outdoor tree height is not an indoor/container estimate.

spacing.reason: Landscape spacing is not pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor sun is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Loquat
summary: An evergreen shrub or tree with leathery, toothed leaves and yellow-orange edible fruit. Flowering and fruiting are cold-sensitive; no cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Eriobotrya japonica and includes Mespilus japonica among synonyms. NC State notes Japanese plum can also mean Prunus salicina; this record is not that plum.

growth.short: Evergreen shrub or tree with leathery, toothed leaves
growth.guidance: NC State describes a tropical evergreen shrub or tree, usually 10–25 ft tall and wide in its landscape profile, with large leathery, toothed leaves. It usually does not fruit in North Carolina because of cold sensitivity; the profile also notes its rounded form can be trained as an espalier.

cultivation.short: Warm site; protect blooms and fruit from cold
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun (with partial shade tolerated) and moist, well-drained soil. It reports blooms or fruit likely will not survive below 28°F although the tree may survive to about 10°F. These are landscape/regional facts, not an indoor-light or hydroponic claim.

harvest.short: Fruit set depends on winter temperatures
harvest.guidance: NC State describes spring-display fruit as yellow-orange, pear-shaped and about 1–2 inches, with edible flesh. The source lists spring as its harvest season and notes cold can prevent flowering/fruit from surviving; do not treat that regional season as a universal date.

propagation.short: NC State lists stem cuttings; no step-by-step protocol is supplied
propagation.guidance: NC State lists stem cutting as a recommended propagation strategy for this species. The page does not give a rooting procedure, timing or success conditions, so those details remain unspecified rather than inferred from another Rosaceae fruit tree.

problems.short: Watch for fire blight; seeds have a specific ingestion caution
problems.guidance: NC State identifies fire blight and other leaf/fruit diseases as concerns. It also flags the seeds: the low-severity poisoning warning applies to eating large quantities of cracked seed pits/kernels, not ordinary handling of the edible flesh. Do not crack or eat the kernels; seek medical advice for an actual ingestion concern.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: A landscape profile for a fruit tree does not establish indoor hydroponics.

growthHabits.reason: The source describes shrub/tree forms; no single value fits the current compatibility habit vocabulary.

name: Chinese Jujube
summary: A deciduous, often thorny fruit tree whose fruit changes from crisp and apple-like when green to date-like when mature. No named cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ziziphus jujuba Mill. and lists Ziziphus zizyphus as a synonym. NC State uses common jujuba and Chinese date; this does not identify a named variety.

growth.short: Deciduous thorny tree or large shrub
growth.guidance: NC State reports a rounded or vase-shaped plant about 15–30 ft tall with thorny branches; it is a landscape-scale plant, not a compact container form.

cultivation.short: Warm, somewhat dry climate; sun to partial shade
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports preference for warm, somewhat dry climates and well-drained but moist soil; the species tolerates drought and poor soils. This does not establish indoor hydroponic performance.

care.short: Expect root suckers; pruning can constrain tree size
care.guidance: UF/IFAS reports that Chinese jujube commonly produces root suckers, sometimes emerging several feet from the parent tree, and that pruning can constrain its 15–30 ft height. Central-leader and open-center forms are described as orchard training systems; the source does not prescribe a universal home pruning schedule or a specific sucker-removal method.

harvest.short: Fruit matures from crisp green to date-like brown-purple
harvest.guidance: NC State describes green fruit with apple-like texture that matures to wrinkled brown-purple fruit, eaten fresh, dried or cooked. In its northern regions the growing season may be too short for fruit set.

propagation.short: NC State lists grafting, seed and stem cutting as routes
propagation.guidance: NC State's species page lists grafting, seed and stem cutting as propagation strategies, but gives no step-by-step method or conditions for any of them. This documents possible routes only; a home propagation protocol remains unspecified.

growthHabits.reason: Rounded and vase-shaped tree forms are not represented by the current compatibility habit vocabulary.

name: Hardy Kiwi
summary: A vigorous, smooth-skinned edible kiwi vine distinct from fuzzy kiwifruit. Many plants require male and female vines to fruit; sex and cultivar are unspecified.

identity.short: Accepted species; cultivar and sex unspecified
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Actinidia arguta. NC State notes several varieties and cultivars; this profile represents only the species, not a named selection or sexed plant.

growth.guidance: NC State says garden vines can grow around 30 ft in a year. A sturdy structure is needed for the vine and fruit; this is not a compact container claim.

cultivation.short: Sun to partial shade; fertile, well-drained soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends full sun to partial shade and well-drained fertile soil. Outdoor pruning guidance is not converted into an indoor trellis or pod-spacing rule.

management.short: Prune in winter and control long shoots in summer
management.guidance: NC State recommends pruning each stem in winter back to 8–10 buds and pruning in summer as needed to control overlong branches. The page does not specify a training system or cultivar-specific schedule, so this remains species-level guidance.

harvest.short: Small smooth-skinned fruit is eaten whole
harvest.guidance: NC State describes grape-sized fruit that need not be peeled and is sweeter and less acidic than fuzzy kiwi. Fruit production commonly needs male and female plants; sex is unknown for an unspecified plant.

propagation.short: Seed and cuttings listed; partial cold-stratification fact only
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and stem cuttings and reports 1–2 months of cold stratification. It does not give complete sowing depth, germination window or seedling care, so no Seed Profile is created.

problems.short: Manage vigorous growth; root rot can occur
problems.guidance: NC State notes the vine can become weedy, cats may damage foliage and roots, and root rot can occur.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Outdoor climbing-vine guidance does not establish indoor hydroponics.

growthHabits.reason: Climbing vine form is not represented by the current compatibility habit vocabulary; no near-equivalent is inferred.

name: Red Mulberry
summary: A deciduous North American tree with edible fruit when ripe and wildlife value. Fruiting is not assured for an unspecified individual because male and female flowers usually occur on separate trees; unripe fruit and milky sap carry safety warnings.

identity.short: Accepted species; distinct from white mulberry
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Morus rubra. This entry is not Morus alba or a named fruiting selection.

growth.short: Deciduous tree with dense, spreading crown
growth.guidance: NC State describes a tree with a dense, spreading landscape crown. Its alternate, toothed leaves may be heart-shaped and range from unlobed to deeply lobed; young shoots more often carry lobed leaves, while canopy leaves are more often unlobed. Leaves turn yellow in fall. Summer fruit attracts wildlife and can stain hard surfaces when it drops.

cultivation.short: Rich, moist, well-drained soil; sun to partial shade
cultivation.guidance: NC State reports best growth in rich, moist, well-drained soil and full sun to partial shade; the species does poorly in poor soil. This outdoor tree profile does not establish indoor cultivation.

maintenance.short: Prune in late fall or winter to limit bleeding
maintenance.guidance: NC State recommends pruning in late fall or winter to avoid bleeding from cuts. This is species-level landscape-tree guidance; it does not establish a special fruiting-pruning system or a container-tree form for this identity.

harvest.short: Consume fruit only when fully ripe
harvest.guidance: NC State describes the fruit as changing from reddish to dark purple as it matures; eat it only when fully ripe, since the source warns that unripe fruit is poisonous. Ripe fruit can be eaten fresh or used in preserves, but has a short shelf life. Fruit color and timing here are species-level North Carolina observations, not a local calendar.

propagation.short: Seed and cuttings listed; seed-starting protocol absent
propagation.guidance: NC State lists seed and stem cuttings but gives no seed-starting procedure. Seed is a possible route; germination requirements remain undocumented here.

problems.short: Unripe fruit and sap have toxicity cautions
problems.guidance: NC State warns that unripe fruit and milky sap may cause hallucinations and stomach upset, and notes that sap can cause contact dermatitis. Its regional list includes borers, whiteflies, bacterial blight that can kill foliage or branches, coral-spot cankers associated with twig dieback, and other possible pests or diseases. These are monitoring cues, not a diagnosis or a prediction that every tree will be affected; dropped fruit and self-seeding can also create maintenance issues.

flowering.short: Small greenish catkin-like flowers appear in spring
flowering.guidance: NC State describes small, pale-green, unisexual flowers in drooping catkin-like spikes in spring. The account gives April–May for North Carolina; local bloom timing can differ.

pollination.short: Male and female flowers usually occur on separate trees
pollination.guidance: NC State reports that male and female flowers usually occur on separate red mulberry trees. This catalog identity does not specify the sex of an individual tree or a compatible pollen source, so fruit production should not be assumed for one unidentified specimen.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Landscape tree guidance does not establish indoor hydroponics.

evidence.note: NC State describes a dense, spreading tree.

spacing.reason: Outdoor canopy spacing is not pod spacing.
